title: Putting a Temperature on Electron Correlation
authors: Paul G. Graf, Florian Matz, Markus Penz, Christian Schilling
abstract: It is common wisdom that a better understanding of how to quantify electron correlation should lead to more efficient treatments of the correlation problem. Here, we not only substantiate this view but turn it into a concrete, systematic framework for ground states. Since prominent correlation measures such as the nonfreeness depend only on the one-particle reduced density matrix, modeling the correlation energy as a function of such a measure naturally places the framework within reduced density matrix functional theory, while keeping the cost at mean-field level. Strikingly, the variable conjugate to the measure emerges as a ``correlation temperature'', thereby connecting correlation measures, functional theory, and effective temperatures. The framework rationalizes methods such as i-DMFT, and we illustrate its key concepts analytically for the Hubbard dimer and numerically for small molecular systems. This brings a fundamental question within reach: how much of the correlation problem can be solved at mean-field cost?
summary: This paper introduces a systematic theoretical framework to tackle electron correlation by expressing the correlation energy as a function of a single, measurable quantity derived from the one-particle reduced density matrix (1RDM). This approach connects correlation measures, Reduced Density Matrix Functional Theory (RDMFT), and the concept of an effective 'correlation temperature'. It offers a path to solving complex correlation problems while maintaining computational efficiency at the mean-field level.
main_problem: The central challenge is developing a systematic, computationally tractable framework to quantify and treat electron correlation energy in many-electron systems.
main_result: The authors propose modeling the correlation energy as a functional of a single correlation measure derived from the one-particle reduced density matrix (1RDM), introducing the concept of a 'correlation temperature'.
method: The framework utilizes Reduced Density Matrix Functional Theory (RDMFT), approximating the correlation functional by making it dependent only on a chosen correlation measure ($\zeta$) derived from the 1RDM.
model_or_system: The theory is developed for general N-electron systems, using the Hartree-Fock method as a starting point. Specific illustrations include the Hubbard dimer and small molecular systems.
key_observables: One-particle reduced density matrix (1RDM), Non-Orthogonal Natural Occupation Numbers (NONs), Nonfreeness ($\zeta_{nf}$), and the 'correlation temperature' ($\kappa_c$).
important_parameters: The correlation measure $\zeta$ and the corresponding correlation temperature $\kappa_c$.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the correlation energy can be effectively parameterized by a single, well-defined correlation measure derived from the 1RDM, allowing the cost to remain at the mean-field level.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the conceptual link between a correlation measure $\zeta(\gamma)$ of the 1RDM, the coarse-grained correlation functional $	ilde{F}_c(\zeta)$, and the correlation temperature $\kappa_c$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the necessity of quantifying correlation via the 1RDM. It then develops the systematic framework by defining the correlation energy functional in terms of a measure $\zeta$. Finally, it illustrates the concepts analytically for the Hubbard dimer and numerically for molecular systems.
why_interesting: The connection drawn between correlation measures, functional theory, and effective temperatures provides a powerful, unifying theoretical lens for understanding correlation effects in condensed matter systems, potentially simplifying complex many-body calculations.
